newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Salzburg Festival moving with the times.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Salzburg Festival moving with the times.

text.p: If this year's ticket sales are anything to go by, Salzburg's music festival has lost none of its lustre by ditching its ultra-conservative image and embracing modern composers.
Three major 20th century operas mark a trend away from the classical tradition of Mozart's birthplace to a broader event.

The Salzburg Festival, founded 77 years ago, opens on Sunday. The six-week programme includes Debussy's "Pelleas et Melisande", Berg's "Wozzeck" and Ligeti's "Le Grande Macabre" -- the latter in a reworked version directed by the charismatic U.S. opera director Peter Sellars.
Although the performances are not sold out, the organisers boast that only tickets in most expensive categories remain unsold. Latecomers will have to pay 4,000 schillings ($500) a seat.

A visit to the Salzburg Festival, held against the backdrop of one of Austria's most beautiful baroque cities, is not cheap. But festival patrons are not short of money, spending on average 22,000 shillings on tickets alone.

"We have experienced many festival visitors bringing along their children and grandchildren," said Andreas Vrtal, head of the festival ticket bureau. "That makes about 100,000 schillings for a family, just for tickets".

Regular festival goers make up 85 percent of all visitors. And with an audience that is getting younger each year, this figure looks secure, especially when one takes into account the dynastic nature of high culture in Salzburg.
"In some performances, three generations of the same family sit united -- love for the festival is inherited," says Vrtal.
SPIN-OFFS FOR LOCAL ECONOMY

During an average stay of nine days, visitors provide spin-offs worth around 2.4 billion schillings to the local economy, according to the Austrian Chamber of Commerce. That figure is significantly more than the 300 million schillings the festival nets in ticket sales.
Peter Schwaiger, manufacturer of traditional Austrian clothing, says the annual event is vital to business.
The cream of Austrian society still like to attend performances in full Austrian regalia -- hand embroidered "Dirndl" dresses for women and formal jackets for men.

But increasingly Salzburg's couturiers are making a healthy living from tourists from Germany, Italy, the United States and fellow Austrians who provide a steady flow of orders for the rural "Landhaus" wear.
Schwaiger moves with the times.
"Sales of the formal, festive costume have dropped, but the "Landhaus" line is doing very well."
While private interest in Austria's prime cultural showcase remains strong, the festival has seen commercial support dwindle.
Companies that used to treat their higher echelons to a few days at the Salzburg festivities as a perk are now faced with corporate spending cuts.
"Companies have to save", says Vrtal. "Bookings have clearly decreased. Ten or even five years ago it was very different."
This has hit the high-priced ticket sector, to the dismay of the organizers.
Festival director Gerard Mortier, an ardent modernist from Belgium, counts on the classical Mozart programme to provide the funds for his forays into 20th century music.

Mortier recently admitted that this year's production of "The Magic Flute" in the Felsenreitschule, a theatre normally reserved for drama, would serve as a cash cow enabling him to stage a more progressive repertoire.
Last year he successfully risked a Schoenberg opera and reckons the audience will be ripe for work by composers such as Janacek and the German Hans Werner Henze by the end of the millennium.

Following a break with eminent figures who have since relinquished their key positions at the festival, Mortier plans to work with a younger generation of directors and artists, giving prominence to the premieres of contemporary work.

For 1998 he already has U.S. film director Hal Hartley working on a rock opera, and has lined up Austria's controversial "angry young woman" writer Elfriede Jelinek for the literary programme. Mortier is also negotiating with David Bowie for cooperation on a thematic project for the year 2000.
This does not mean that Salzburg is neglecting the classics.
Mozart's work remains a major focus -- five operas this year -- while Schubert's bicentenary is to be celebrated with a cycle of concerts directed by Claudio Abbado.

However, even Mozart is entering the digital age. A co-producution with Salzburg's avant-garde festival, "Sommerszene", features an Internet compatible version of "Il Seraglio" in which the hero searches a digital network for his abducted lover.
